# Finance is a story about money changing hands at different times

The first question in any financial problem is **not which complicated model to choose**. It is: **Who gives whom how much money, and when?**

If you can draw the money on a timeline, then we can explain discounting, bond valuation, yield curves, portfolio risk and derivatives step by step.

This course uses **three books you provided**: David G. Luenberger, *Investment Science* (1st and 2nd editions), and Frank J. Fabozzi (ed.), *The Handbook of Fixed Income Securities*, 8th edition. It follows their concepts but uses **entirely original explanations and numerical teaching examples**, not copied textbook passages. See the [reading and source map](guides/books-and-learning-map.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## Our recurring example: one very small bond

You lend **100** today. You receive **5** in year one and **105** in year two. We will reuse this until the ideas feel natural. A bond is not difficult because of its name; it is a set of dated cash flows.
:::

## 1. Financial Foundations — understand every number

[**Start here: Financial Foundations**](foundations/index.qmd)

Learn cash-flow timelines → compounding → present value → NPV/IRR → no arbitrage → holding-period return.

**Question to answer:** Why is receiving 105 next year worth 100 today when the appropriate annual rate is 5%?

## 2. Fixed Income — value the promised payments

[**Fixed Income: Bonds, Curves and Risk**](fixed-income/index.qmd)

From the [interactive bond price experiment](fixed-income/bond-pricing.qmd), continue through quoted yields, accrued interest, spot rates, bootstrapping, forward rates, [duration](fixed-income/duration.qmd), convexity, DV01, immunisation, credit, embedded options, MBS and floaters.

**Question to answer:** Why does a bond's price decline when its required yield increases, and how much can it decline?

## 3. Portfolio Theory — decisions involving more than one asset

[**Portfolio Construction and Risk**](portfolio/index.qmd)

Understand expected returns, covariance and correlation, Markowitz portfolio choice, CAPM beta, benchmark tracking error, VaR, expected shortfall and performance attribution.

**Question to answer:** How can combining two risky assets produce less volatility than an average of their individual volatilities?

## 4. Derivatives — the value of agreements and choices

[**Forwards, Swaps, Options and Hedges**](derivatives/index.qmd)

Start with a simple forward agreement, then understand swapping fixed and floating coupons, an option's one-period price, and why half a share plus a loan can replicate a call payoff in a two-state model.

**Question to answer:** Why can an option have value even when its owner may choose never to use it?

## A formula is not an explanation until you substitute numbers

$$
PV=\frac{105}{1+0.05}=100
$$

**What every symbol means:** $PV$ is present value; 105 is the money received in exactly one year; 0.05 is the suitable one-year discount rate written as a decimal.

**Calculate it:** 105/1.05=100. If you already have 100 today, investing at 5% gives the same 105 next year. That is the intuition behind present value.

Our rule is universal: **story → timeline → equation → every symbol explained → numerical substitution → small code → what can go wrong.** We never introduce mathematics just to look sophisticated.

## Run the entire financial calculator

~~~bash
python3 finance/examples/finance_lab.py
python3 -m unittest discover -s finance/examples -p 'test_*.py'
~~~

The [single original Python file](examples/finance_lab.py) and its [unit tests](examples/test_finance_lab.py) use only Python's standard library. Production trading models need many more conventions; the lab intentionally isolates each finance idea.
